newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia Surgut oil firm sale to secure owners' hold.
newsitem.headline: Russia Surgut oil firm sale to secure owners' hold.

text.p: Russia's tough terms for selling 40 percent of oil giant Surgut Holding next month practically guarantee that no outsiders will be able to buy into the prize oil company, energy analysts said on Wednesday.

"This is not an unusual way to go forward," said Stephen O'Sullivan, associate director of oil and gas at London-based MC Securities, commenting on auction terms that make it nearly impossible for anyone other than Surgut to snap up the stake.
Surgut Holding is one of a dozen or so vertically-integrated oil groups created over the last few years.
Its main production unit AO Surgutneftegaz is one of Russia's top oil producers and a favourite with foreign investors.
But outside investors are not likely to gain footholds into Surgut Holding, also called NK Surgutneftegaz, when the 40.12 percent, four million share stake is auctioned on February 25.
The stake is currently under management by Surgut's pension fund, which won the right to manage the shares in the first of Russia's controversial shares-for-loans auctions in 1995.
The shares-for-loans scheme was set up to offer management rights for government stakes in prize companies in exchange for loans to the cash-strapped government.
Now the time has come to auction the stake -- and, like the shares-for-loans scheme, the winners appear to be predetermined, analysts said.

The February auction will almost certainly involve Surgut buying the stake, since no other potential bidders can meet the auction's condition that bidders already hold a five percent stake in the Surgutneftegaz production unit, oil analysts said.

The auction -- which mirrors recent government sales of stakes in other big oil firms -- could once again raise charges that Russia is offering significant stakes in its best companies to a narrow circle of financial and industrial powerhouses.
O'Sullivan said recent sales of government-owned oil company stakes had more or less been designed to keep the companies' current shareholder structures in place.
Under the terms of the Surgut sale, bidders must offer at least 410 billion roubles ($73 million) for the shares and 1.2 trillion roubles in investment.
Still, some analysts said the sale would not hurt current outside shareholders in Surgut, which owns the strategically positioned Kirishi oil refinery near St Petersburg.
"Investors could interpret it as a move towards lack of transparency," said Salomon Brothers oil and gas analyst Elena Merkoulova. "But as a strategic move, it is slightly positive.

"Surgut can float the shares, use them as collateral, and, most importantly, they can avoid risk of the government raising enough money to buy back the stake. It will be a private oil company," she said.
But the sale may fail to raise the investment funds Russian oil firms need to reverse years of steep output declines.
O'Sullivan said the investments required under the tender may vanish in accounting books when Surgut buys itself.
"There is always the question whether the investment will actually be made," said.
The Kremlin is not likely to reap rewards from the sale, since the starting price is about the same as the loan offered by the Surgut pension fund to the government in 1995.
But some still see the newest stage in the privatisation of Russia's leading oil majors as a step back into the Byzantine world of Russia's rocky transition to a market economy.
"When they announced shares-for-loans in the middle of 1995, nobody expected it to be quite as open as a tender for Exxon shares," O'Sullivan said.
($1=5627 Rouble)
